page: Vultr voc-s-1c-8gb-150s-amd is an Optimized Cloud Compute server instance featuring a single dedicated AMD EPYC physical core on the x86_64 architecture. Operating at a clock speed of 2.0 GHz, the processor includes 32 KB of L1d cache, 1.0 MB of L2 cache, and 32 MB of L3 cache. The hardware configuration is equipped with 8.0 GB of system memory, providing a 1:8 vCPU-to-RAM ratio. Local storage consists of a bundled 150 GB NVMe SSD, and the instance includes one complimentary public IPv4 address. No GPU accelerators are present.

Benchmark data reveals a stark contrast between single-core and multi-core performance due to the single-vCPU limitation. In stress-ng testing, single-core CPU performance ranks in the top 10%, and single-threaded gzip and bzip3 decompression speeds are in the top 25%. However, multi-core CPU performance in stress-ng and Geekbench falls into the bottom 25% and bottom 10% respectively. Memory bandwidth for large blocks is average, while small-block cached read bandwidth is weak. Complex multi-threaded tasks, such as software compilation, ray tracing, and image processing, score in the bottom 10% of benchmarks.

From a qualitative cost-efficiency perspective, this instance offers dedicated CPU allocation and high memory density per core, making it a viable option for workloads that require guaranteed CPU cycles without the overhead of multi-threaded scaling. It is suited for lightweight single-threaded applications, basic text processing, and small-scale memory-intensive tasks. However, it is poorly suited for database operations, high-throughput static web serving, or parallel processing workloads, as indicated by low scores in Redis SET operations and Passmark database tests.
description: Vultr voc-s-1c-8gb-150s-amd is an Optimized Cloud Compute instance featuring a single dedicated AMD EPYC core running at 2.0 GHz on the x86_64 architecture. It is configured with 8.0 GB of RAM, a 150 GB NVMe SSD, and one public IPv4 address, with no GPU acceleration. Performance benchmarks show a significant divergence: single-core CPU performance is highly competitive, ranking in the top 10% for stress-ng, while multi-core and parallel processing metrics fall into the bottom 10% to 25% due to the single-vCPU constraint. Memory bandwidth and text processing perform at average levels, but database operations and static web serving throughput are weak. This instance is qualitatively cost-efficient for memory-dense, single-threaded tasks, making it suitable for lightweight background utilities, basic text processing, and small-scale single-core workloads rather than parallelized applications or high-traffic databases.
